prediction_ref.short_label: Durable ask-user checkpoints become a standard harness primitive by H1 2027

validation_rows.evidence_summary: Today showed what a single, non-durable consent decision costs. The repository-supplied entries that fire on session start and folder open are gated by one workspace-trust choice, taken once, at the moment someone is trying to start work, about a folder they cloned on purpose — and today's account is blunt that people click through because clicking through is what the product is for. What that implies a harness would need is a checkpoint that survives past the first click and returns at the moment an entry would actually execute, itemised rather than blanket, or entries held inert until enabled deliberately. Neither of the two products named in the reporting, Claude Code and Visual Studio Code, is described as having anything beyond the trust decision, and no harness shipped such a primitive today.

prediction_ref.short_label: Tailscale defaults reusable auth keys to a bounded node count by H1 2027

validation_rows.evidence_summary: Today is the credential-blast-radius argument in its most concrete form. The payload swept npm tokens, GitHub credentials of every flavour including short-lived OIDC tokens, AWS keys and instance-metadata credentials, Kubernetes service-account tokens, Vault, Stripe and Slack keys, SSH keys, Docker configs and Terraform state, then republished itself through any publish token it found — propagation ran on credentials that carried no bound on what they could do next, which is why the movement between organisations was measured in minutes rather than days. The remediation has the same shape: every organisation that pulled a poisoned version now rotates across publishing tokens, cloud keys, cluster tokens and secret-store credentials, a sweep that touches systems a company cannot pause. Tailscale is not mentioned in today's material, no networking vendor changed a key default, and nothing today concerned node-count limits specifically.

prediction_ref.short_label: Sub-2-bit quantization fits a second 20B-class model under 5 GB by Q2 2027

validation_rows.evidence_summary: The memory target was cleared today by a different mechanism, at four times the parameter count. Swiftlet reports Qwen3-Next-80B — 42 gigabytes of weights on disk — peaking at 4.3 gigabytes of resident memory on an M5 Mac, and a 35-billion Qwen3.6 at 2.6 gigabytes, with the same model on an iPhone 17 in about 2.5 gigabytes. It gets there not by compressing further but by keeping only the dense part resident at four bits and streaming routed experts off storage into a user-sized cache. Today's account is explicit that the mechanism is architectural rather than a new quantisation, and the bit width it does state covers the dense layers only, with nothing said about how the streamed experts are stored. No sub-2-bit result, and no 20-billion-class model under 5 gigabytes by compression, appears in today's material.

bridge.narrative: The five-gigabyte mark fell by the wrong route. Nothing was compressed harder; residency policy changed, dense weights held at four bits while routed experts stream on demand, and an 80-billion model sat under the ceiling a 20-billion model was supposed to reach. bridge.remaining_gap: The stated bit width covers dense layers only, and a rate near five tokens a second is not the same job as a portable model.
